sections.h2: What an Ohio quitclaim deed transfers
sections.html:
A quitclaim hands over whatever the signer holds and nothing beyond it. R.C. 5301.02 treats a grant of land as conveying the full interest the grantor can lawfully pass, unless the deed plainly shows a smaller estate was meant. Quitclaim wording adds no extra title. A grantor who owns half gives the grantee half.

The Revised Code prints statutory forms for three other deed types, each with named promises. The general warranty form in R.C. 5302.05 carries covenants that the grantor owns the land in fee simple, that nothing encumbers it, and that the grantor will defend the title against all claims. The limited warranty form in 5302.07 shrinks those promises to claims arising through the grantor. The fiduciary form in 5302.09 serves executors, administrators, trustees, guardians and receivers.

Covenants only come along when the deed says so. Under R.C. 5302.06 the phrase "general warranty covenants" brings in the full list of promises. Leave that phrase out and the buyer is relying on the title the grantor actually has.

sections.h2: Signing, witnessing and what the deed should contain
sections.html:
The grantor's signature has to be acknowledged. R.C. 5301.01 lists who can take the acknowledgment: a judge or clerk of a state court of record, the county auditor, the county engineer, a notary public or a mayor. That official certifies it over his or her own signature. Most owners just visit a notary.

The statutory forms show what a tidy Ohio deed looks like. It names the grantor with marital status and county, recites consideration, gives the grantee's tax-mailing address, describes the land, cites the earlier recorded instrument by volume and page, and includes dower release language for a spouse. Those elements make a sound checklist for any deed you prepare.

One duty catches sellers of troubled houses. Under R.C. 5301.253, an owner who has received a written building or housing code violation notice must give the grantee written notice of those violations before any transfer agreement is made. With no written agreement, the notice is due before the deed is filed. A notice already sitting in an issuing authority's public records also follows the property to later owners without a fresh order.

sections.h2: Where an Ohio deed is filed and what the recorder charges
sections.html:
Take the deed to the recorder in the county where the parcel lies, as R.C. 5301.25 directs. Skipping this leaves a gap: an unrecorded deed is treated as fraudulent against a later buyer who paid in good faith and knew nothing of it.

The recorder's price list is in R.C. 317.32. For recording and indexing a standard instrument, the statute prints these charges:

  • Seventeen dollars as a base fee plus seventeen dollars as a housing trust fund fee covers the first two pages.
  • Every later page adds four dollars of each.
  • A county may add a preservation surcharge of no more than five dollars.

The auditor looks at the deed before the recorder does. If a surveyor drew the land, the auditor requires the deed to name the surveyor in one short sentence: "A survey of this property was made by" followed by the name.

sections.h2: Who pays the conveyance fee on a quitclaim?
sections.html:
The person giving up title pays. Under R.C. 319.202, the grantor covers the state-set fee plus any county transfer tax when the statement of value reaches the auditor. R.C. 319.54 sets the mandatory fee at one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is higher.

A county can pile its own tax on top. R.C. 322.02 allows up to thirty cents per hundred dollars, charged to the grantor and paid to the auditor before the deed goes to the recorder. Ask your auditor whether your county levies it.

The definition of "value" matters. On a sale it means everything paid, including any mortgage balance. On a gift in whole or part it means the price the land would likely bring on the open market. Deliberately misstating value is forbidden. Separately, a fifty-cent charge applies to each transfer or entry on the auditor's books and is paid by whoever requests it.

sections.h2: Transfers exempt from the conveyance fee
sections.html:
Quite a few are, and several match what families do with quitclaims. When an exemption fits, the form only needs a short note giving the reason.

Selected exemptions under R.C. 319.54(G)(3)
Type of transferLetter in the statute
Confirming or correcting a deed already recorded(c)
Gift between spouses, or from parent to child or the spouse of either(d)
Made under court order, when not a result of a sale under that order(f)
No money or other valuable consideration paid, and not a gift(m)
Among heirs or devisees of one decedent with no money paid(s)
To a trustee when the grantor kept an unlimited power to revoke(t)
Sale for delinquent taxes or assessments(e)

The full list in section 319.54 is longer. It also reaches government transfers, transfers that only secure or release a debt, and assorted corporate and trust moves.

sections.h2: Survivorship and transfer on death instead of a quitclaim
sections.html:
When a family wants a transfer to take effect at death, Ohio offers statutory tools that a plain quitclaim cannot match. R.C. 5302.20 creates a survivorship tenancy when a deed or will shows clear intent that the survivor takes everything. The word "or" between two grantees is not enough alone. If fewer than all survivorship tenants convey to an outsider, the grantor's interest passes only if the grantor survives.

A transfer on death designation affidavit under R.C. 5302.22 lets an owner name beneficiaries who take title at death. No payment and no handoff to the beneficiary is needed. The affidavit must be on file with the recorder before the owner dies, at the same recording price as a deed, and it is sworn before someone authorized to administer oaths.

Two more survivorship rules touch family deeds. A conveyance from every survivorship tenant to another person, or from all but one of them to the remaining tenant, ends the tenancy and vests title in the grantee. And if the only two tenants are spouses whose marriage ends by divorce, annulment or dissolution, the title becomes a tenancy in common unless the judgment says survivorship continues.

A quitclaim made now gives the grantee a present interest, and the exemptions in the table above cover family gifts. By any route, a deed does not clear taxes. The lien statute keeps the year's claim on the parcel until it is paid. If you plan to sell, get the treasurer's payoff figure before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Ohio house with a quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Yes, any signed, acknowledged and recorded deed can carry a sale. The buyer gets only the title you hold, with none of the covenants a warranty form carries. Ask your title company which form the buyer's lender will accept.

faqs.q: Does an Ohio quitclaim deed have to be notarized?
faqs.a: The signature must be acknowledged before an official the statute names, and a notary public is one of them. Most owners use a notary.

faqs.q: Will a quitclaim deed erase a mortgage or tax lien in Ohio?
faqs.a: No. The year's tax lien attaches on January 1 and stays until paid, no matter who holds title. Get payoff numbers from the treasurer and your lender before you transfer.

faqs.q: Is there a conveyance fee on a deed between relatives?
faqs.a: Gifts between spouses, and gifts from a parent to a child or a child's spouse, are on the exempt list. So is a transfer where nothing of value changes hands and it is not a gift. The form carries a short statement of the reason.

faqs.q: Where do I record an Ohio quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: Bring it to the recorder in the county that holds the parcel, once the auditor has endorsed it. Until then a later good faith buyer can win out over it. The recorder's office can quote its charges.
